claims.text: Wear resistance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is primarily governed by formation of an adherent protective oxide film during sliding.
An oxygen-containing sliding environment generates the protective oxide film.
The oxide film acts as a barrier that reduces direct contact with the underlying alloy.
Reduced direct contact due to the oxide film decreases abrasive wear of the underlying alloy.
The initial coating is compositionally homogeneous.
The initial coating surface has little pre-existing oxide.
Changing the wear-test atmosphere from inert gas to an oxygen-rich gas will promote oxidation during wear.
The oxide film formed during sliding is nanostructured and adherent.
In an inert environment, suppression of the oxide film causes greater wear through direct mechanical action.
At otherwise identical test conditions, an oxygen-rich atmosphere will produce a significantly lower wear rate than an inert atmosphere.
The oxygen-rich test will produce a more continuous and stable oxide film than the inert-atmosphere test.
The proposed mechanism applies at moderate sliding speeds and temperatures that preserve oxide stability and avoid thermal degradation.
The proposed mechanism applies over oxygen partial pressures that form a protective oxide without excessive oxide growth.
Very high temperatures or oxygen levels may cause brittle oxide growth and fall outside the mechanism's valid range.
Oxide thickness, composition, and mechanical integrity may vary with alloy composition and wear-test conditions.
The magnitude of wear reduction may differ among high-entropy-alloy systems.
Parallel inert and oxygen-enriched wear tests will use the same coating and identical load, speed, duration, and temperature.
The hypothesis is designated as falsified if oxygen-rich tests show neither a statistically significant wear decrease nor evidence of a protective oxide film.
